description: How public money is raised through taxation and spent on welfare, health, education and care.
content_html:
Why Does Government Collect Tax?

Governments need money to run public services — things such as schools, hospitals, roads, the police and welfare benefits. This money is raised primarily through taxation. In the UK, central government collects most taxes, and some funding is also raised by local councils through the council tax. Without taxation, the government would be unable to provide the services that citizens rely on throughout their lives.

The UK government collects tax in several different ways. Income tax is paid by people who earn above a certain threshold — in 2024–25 the personal allowance (the amount you can earn before paying income tax) was £12,570. National Insurance is another tax on earnings that funds state benefits and the NHS. Value Added Tax (VAT) is charged at 20 per cent on most goods and services and is paid indirectly by consumers when they make purchases. Corporation tax is paid by businesses on their profits.

Key Fact

The four main forms of UK taxation are: income tax (on earnings), National Insurance (on earnings, funds benefits and the NHS), VAT (on most goods and services at 20%), and corporation tax (on company profits). Local government also raises money through council tax on residential properties.

How Is Public Money Spent?

The UK government sets out its spending plans in the annual Budget, presented to Parliament by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The largest areas of public spending are typically health (principally the National Health Service), social protection (welfare benefits and pensions), and education. Together these three areas account for the majority of government expenditure. Other significant areas include defence, transport infrastructure, and debt interest payments on money the government has borrowed in previous years.

Local government also spends public money, funded partly by central government grants and partly by council tax. Local councils provide services including waste collection, local roads, social care for the elderly and disabled, planning, and early-years education. The budgeting process at both national and local level involves difficult trade-offs: increasing spending in one area often means cutting or holding back spending in another.

Supporters of generous welfare spending argue that a comprehensive welfare state ensures that no citizen is left without support during illness, unemployment, or old age. They contend that investment in welfare reduces poverty and inequality, generates social cohesion, and prevents the long-term costs associated with untreated mental and physical illness. They often point to the post-war settlement that created the NHS and the modern benefits system as evidence of what collective provision can achieve.

Critics of high welfare spending argue that an overly generous benefits system can reduce incentives to work and places a heavy burden on taxpayers and public debt. They suggest that welfare programmes must be means-tested and targeted at those most in need, rather than provided universally, in order to keep costs sustainable. They argue that a growing national debt creates long-term risks for the economy and future generations.

Both viewpoints reflect genuine political values about the role of the state, individual responsibility, and the balance between rights and responsibilities. There is no single “correct” answer to these debates — they form part of the ongoing democratic conversation about how public money should be used.

Health, Education and Elderly Care

The NHS provides healthcare free at the point of use to all UK residents, funded by taxation and National Insurance. It is the largest single item of day-to-day public spending. Supporters of this model argue that universal free healthcare prevents a two-tier system where only the wealthy can afford good treatment. Critics argue that the NHS faces growing demand from an ageing population and that funding pressures require either higher taxes or a different funding model.

Education is funded largely through central government grants to schools, with additional funding channelled through local authorities. Early years, primary, secondary, and further education are all publicly funded, though there is ongoing debate about how university tuition should be funded — whether primarily through student loans, general taxation, or a combination of the two.

The social care system supports elderly and disabled people who need help with daily living. Unlike the NHS, social care is not entirely free at the point of use — individuals may need to contribute to the costs of residential or home care depending on their savings. This gap between NHS funding and social care funding has been a source of significant political debate, with different parties proposing different solutions.

Key Fact

The three largest areas of UK government spending are health (the NHS), social protection (benefits and pensions), and education. Together they typically account for more than half of all public expenditure. Defence is a significant but smaller budget item.

Governments face the challenge of managing risk when making spending decisions. A sudden economic downturn, a public health emergency, or a natural disaster may require extra spending that was not planned in the annual Budget. To manage this risk, governments may hold reserves, borrow money by issuing government bonds (known as gilts), or adjust tax rates. The budget deficit occurs when spending exceeds tax revenues. When deficits accumulate over time they add to the national debt, which must eventually be repaid through future taxation or spending cuts.

Local councils face similar challenges but with much less room to manoeuvre. Unlike the central government, councils cannot borrow freely or print money. When central government grants are reduced, councils must choose which services to cut or reduce — decisions that directly affect communities and are sometimes highly controversial locally.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on government spending, the most common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that either supports high public spending or criticises it without presenting the opposing view. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, the creation of the NHS, debates about welfare reform, or the distinction between health and social care funding. For a 4-mark “Describe” question, avoid drifting into evaluation; give two clearly described features and develop each one. For source-interpretation questions, do not simply list what the source says — reach a judgement about what it reveals and link it to your own knowledge of taxation or spending priorities.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Taxation — including income tax, National Insurance, VAT and corporation tax — is how government raises the money needed to fund public services. Local government also raises money through council tax.
  • The three largest areas of UK public spending are health (the NHS), social protection (welfare and pensions), and education. Budgeting involves difficult trade-offs because increasing one area of spending often requires cuts elsewhere.
  • There are genuine political debates about how much governments should spend on welfare, health and education, with supporters arguing for collective provision and critics raising concerns about cost, incentives and long-term debt. Extended-response questions expect you to present both sides fairly.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a tax on the income a person earns from employment?
A) Corporation tax
B) Council tax
C) Income tax
D) Value Added Tax
Identify two services that are funded by local government.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct service, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: waste collection; local road maintenance; social care for the elderly or disabled; planning and housing services; early-years or children's services. Two versions of the same service (e.g. 'bins' and 'recycling') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the UK government raises money through taxation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per described way (1 for naming the tax, 1 for describing what it is charged on or how it works). Example: income tax is charged on a person's earnings above the personal allowance (1 mark for naming income tax, 1 mark for describing it as a tax on earnings above a threshold). VAT is charged at 20% on most goods and services when sold (1 for naming VAT, 1 for describing it as a tax on the sale of goods and services). Other valid taxes include National Insurance and corporation tax. Avoid awarding the second mark for vague descriptions such as 'it is paid by everyone'.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional national newspaper published the following extract after the government's annual Budget:

'The Chancellor announced a £3.2 billion increase in NHS funding, to be funded partly by a 2p rise in the basic rate of income tax. Speaking after the statement, the leader of a national taxpayer campaign group said: “This is the right investment — a healthy population is a productive population and the NHS is under enormous pressure.” A spokesperson for a small business organisation responded: “Raising income tax reduces disposable income for workers and increases the pressure on businesses that top up employee pay. There must be a better way to fund the NHS.”'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about the challenges of funding public services?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a tax rise to fund the NHS creates both supporters and critics); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the extract reveals that funding decisions involve trade-offs between service provision and economic burden on taxpayers); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to the general challenge of balancing public need — such as the NHS being the largest area of government spending — with tax burdens and national debt); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and own knowledge (e.g. the source illustrates that there is no politically neutral way to fund public services: both the decision to raise taxes and the decision not to have visible costs and consequences).

practice_questions.text:
A national charity has published a report claiming that cuts to social care funding leave vulnerable elderly people without adequate support.

Discuss whether the government should always prioritise health and social care when deciding how to spend public money.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion presenting both sides with developed points, connective language, at least one named real-world example (e.g. the NHS, the social care funding gap, or the annual Budget process), and a clear overall assessment of which arguments are strongest.

Secure: Both sides covered with some development and at least one named real-world example. A conclusion is reached, though the evaluative judgement may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Relevant points made but mainly one-sided or lacking real-world examples. May list arguments without weighing them.

Emerging: Basic points about spending or health with little development, no named example, and no comparative judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A local pressure group is campaigning for the government to increase income tax to pay for better local social care services for elderly people, arguing that the current funding system is failing those most in need.

Evaluate whether raising income tax is the best way to fund improvements to public services such as social care.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. the NHS funded through National Insurance and income tax, the social care funding gap, VAT as an alternative revenue source, or international models such as social care insurance systems); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided or examples are vague.

Emerging: Basic points about tax or spending with little development; no named real-world example; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in favour: income tax is directly linked to ability to pay (higher earners pay more); it already funds the NHS and could similarly fund social care; raising it ensures a reliable income stream for services. Arguments against: raising income tax reduces disposable income and may reduce work incentives; VAT or corporation tax increases could raise equivalent revenue; alternative models such as insurance-based social care (as in Germany) spread cost differently; increasing borrowing or public-private partnerships may be more politically viable.

knowledge_checks.q: What is VAT charged on in the UK?
options: Most goods and services when sold

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is typically the largest single area of UK government day-to-day spending?
Local councils raise money partly through central government grants and partly through _____ tax on residential properties.
The difference between what a government spends and what it raises in tax in a given year is called the budget _____.
Match each type of tax to what it is charged on:
right: Earnings above a personal allowance threshold
Most goods and services when sold

flashcard_questions.a: Compulsory payments made by individuals and businesses to the government to fund public services.

flashcard_questions.q: What is income tax charged on?
flashcard_questions.a: Earnings from employment or self-employment above the personal allowance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is VAT and at what standard rate is it charged in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: A tax on most goods and services when sold, charged at 20% on standard-rated items.
A tax paid by businesses on their profits.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three largest areas of UK government public spending.
flashcard_questions.a: Health (NHS), social protection (welfare and pensions), and education.
When government spending exceeds tax revenues in a given year.
Support for elderly and disabled people to help them live independently, funded by local councils and health services.

flashcard_questions.q: How is the NHS primarily funded?
flashcard_questions.a: Through general taxation and National Insurance contributions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is budgeting in the context of government?
flashcard_questions.a: The process of allocating public funding across different services within a finite budget.

flashcard_questions.q: How does local government raise money beyond central government grants?
flashcard_questions.a: Through council tax on residential properties.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do governments sometimes need to borrow money?
flashcard_questions.a: To cover a budget deficit when spending exceeds tax revenues in a given year.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one argument in favour of generous welfare spending.
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces poverty and inequality and ensures citizens receive support during illness or unemployment.

glossary_terms.definition: Compulsory payments made by individuals and businesses to the government, used to fund public services.
A tax levied on the income a person earns from employment or self-employment.
A tax added to the price of most goods and services when they are sold, currently set at 20% on standard-rated items in the UK.
The process by which government allocates public funding across different services, balancing competing demands within a finite budget.
Support and assistance provided by local councils and health services to help elderly and disabled people live independently.
The difference between what a government spends and what it raises in tax in a given year.

items.title: More or Less: How Much Does the NHS Cost? — BBC Radio 4
items.description: Tim Harford and the More or Less team fact-check claims about NHS spending, taxation and public service funding. Excellent for understanding how statistics are used (and misused) in spending debates.

items.title: The Rest Is Politics: Who Pays for Britain?
items.description: Campbell and Stewart examine the politics of taxation and public spending, covering income tax, VAT and the trade-offs governments face. Balanced left/right analysis.

items.title: How is Money Created? — Educational explainer
items.description: Clear explainer covering how governments raise money through taxation, borrowing and monetary policy. Good background for understanding budget deficits and national debt.

items.title: The Dirty Secret of Capitalism — Nick Hanauer (TED)
items.description: A wealthy entrepreneur argues that low wages and inequality are a political choice, not an economic inevitability. Useful for evaluating welfare spending debates from a centre-left perspective.

items.title: The Best Stats You've Ever Seen — Hans Rosling (TED)
items.description: Hans Rosling uses live data to challenge misconceptions about wealth, health and public investment worldwide. Excellent for contextualising NHS and welfare spending data.

items.title: I, Daniel Blake (2016)
items.description: Ken Loach's Palme d'Or-winning film following a middle-aged man navigating the UK benefits system after a heart attack. A powerful human account of how welfare policy affects real lives.

items.title: Years and Years (2019 series)
items.description: BBC drama set in the near-future UK, tracing how political and economic decisions about public services ripple through one family's life over fifteen years.

items.title: gov.uk: How Taxes Work
items.description: Official government explanation of income tax, National Insurance, VAT and corporation tax — the four main UK tax types covered in this lesson.

items.title: BBC Bitesize: Government and the Economy
items.description: GCSE Citizenship revision page on taxation, public spending priorities, and the role of central and local government in funding services.

items.title: Institute for Fiscal Studies: UK Public Spending
items.description: The IFS publishes accessible charts and explainers on UK government expenditure, broken down by NHS, education, welfare and other categories. Authoritative, non-partisan data source.
